Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We study the pseudospectrum of a class of non-selfadjoint differential operators. Our work consists in a detailed study of the microlocal properties, which rule the spectral stability or instability phenomena appearing under small perturbations for elliptic quadratic differential operators. The class of elliptic quadratic differential operators stands for the class of operators defined in the Weyl quantization by complex-valued elliptic quadratic symbols. We establish in this paper a simple necessary and sufficient condition on the Weyl symbol of these operators, which ensures the stability of their spectra. When this condition is violated, we prove that it occurs some strong spectral instabilities for the high energies of these operators, in some regions which can be far away from their spectra. We give a precise geometrical description of them, which explains the results obtained for these operators in some numerical simulations giving the computation of false eigenvalues far from their spectra by algorithms for eigenvalues computing.

outputs.L1: We study the pseudospectrum of a class of non-selfadjoint differential operators. Our work provides a detailed analysis of the microlocal properties that govern the spectral stability or instability phenomena arising under small perturbations of elliptic quadratic differential operators. This class consists of operators defined via Weyl quantization by complex-valued elliptic quadratic symbols. In this paper, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition on the Weyl symbols of these operators that ensures the stability of their spectra. When this condition is violated, we prove that strong spectral instabilities occur at high energies for these operators, in certain regions that may lie far from their spectra. We provide a precise geometrical description of these regions, which explains numerical results observed for these operators, including the computation of spurious eigenvalues far from the spectra by eigenvalue algorithms.
outputs.L2:
This work investigates the pseudospectrum of a family of non-selfadjoint differential operators. It provides a thorough analysis of the microlocal features that determine whether the spectra of elliptic quadratic differential operators remain stable or become unstable under small perturbations. Here, elliptic quadratic differential operators are understood as operators obtained through Weyl quantization from complex-valued elliptic quadratic symbols.

In the paper, we prove a straightforward necessary and sufficient condition, formulated in terms of the Weyl symbol, that guarantees spectral stability for these operators. If this condition fails, we show that pronounced spectral instabilities arise at high energies, in certain regions that may lie far from the actual spectrum. We also give an exact geometric characterization of these regions, thereby accounting for numerical observations in which eigenvalue-computing algorithms produce spurious eigenvalues located far away from the true spectra of such operators.
outputs.L3:
The study investigates the pseudospectrum of non-selfadjoint differential operators, with particular emphasis on elliptic quadratic differential operators. Unlike selfadjoint operators, whose spectra are typically stable under small perturbations, non-selfadjoint operators can exhibit highly unstable spectral behavior. In such cases, the pseudospectrum provides a more accurate description of the operator’s behavior than the spectrum alone, since it captures regions of the complex plane where the resolvent becomes large and where small perturbations may create spectral values.

A central focus of the work is the analysis of microlocal properties that govern whether the spectrum of these operators remains stable or becomes unstable under small perturbations. By studying the Weyl symbol associated with the operator, the authors identify the underlying phase-space mechanisms responsible for spectral stability. This microlocal perspective allows them to connect analytic properties of the operator with geometric features of its symbol.

The paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition on the Weyl symbol that guarantees spectral stability for elliptic quadratic differential operators. When this condition is satisfied, the pseudospectrum remains well controlled, and small perturbations do not produce unexpected spectral behavior far from the actual spectrum. In this stable regime, the spectrum gives a reliable picture of the operator’s behavior.

In contrast, when the condition on the Weyl symbol fails, the operators exhibit strong spectral instabilities at high energies. These instabilities can occur in regions of the complex plane that are far removed from the true spectrum. In such regions, the resolvent norm may become very large, meaning that even extremely small perturbations can generate apparent eigenvalues. This reveals that the spectral behavior of non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic operators can be highly sensitive and that the spectrum alone may be misleading.

The authors also use their theoretical results to explain phenomena observed in numerical simulations. In computations involving non-selfadjoint operators, one often encounters spurious or false eigenvalues that appear far from the true spectrum. The paper provides a geometrical explanation for this effect: these false eigenvalues arise in regions of large pseudospectrum, where the operator is especially sensitive to perturbations, including numerical errors. Thus, the study clarifies why numerical approximations may suggest the presence of eigenvalues where none actually exist and shows how pseudospectral geometry accounts for these misleading spectral artifacts.

The study investigates the pseudospectral behavior of a broad class of non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators. These operators are obtained by Weyl quantization of complex-valued elliptic quadratic forms on phase space, and they provide a natural model for understanding instability phenomena in non-selfadjoint spectral theory. Unlike selfadjoint operators, whose spectra typically give reliable information about resolvent behavior, non-selfadjoint operators may exhibit large resolvent norms far away from the spectrum. This makes their spectral analysis delicate and has important consequences for both theory and numerical computation.

The main focus of the work is a detailed microlocal analysis of the Weyl-quantized quadratic symbol associated with such an operator. By examining the geometry of the complex quadratic symbol and its range in the complex plane, the study identifies precisely when the spectrum is stable under small perturbations and when it is not. In particular, it establishes a necessary and sufficient condition, formulated directly in terms of the principal quadratic symbol, that characterizes spectral stability. When this condition is satisfied, the pseudospectrum remains controlled in a suitable sense, and the spectrum accurately reflects the behavior of the resolvent.

When the condition fails, however, the situation changes dramatically. The study proves that strong pseudospectral effects occur at high energies: the resolvent norm becomes extremely large in regions of the complex plane that may lie far from the actual spectrum. These regions correspond to points where the operator behaves, microlocally, as though approximate eigenfunctions exist, even though no genuine eigenvalues are present nearby. As a result, very small perturbations of the operator can produce large shifts in the apparent spectrum.

This phenomenon explains why numerical computations of eigenvalues for non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic operators can produce misleading results. Standard discretization or rounding errors may act as small perturbations, and in the presence of large pseudospectra these perturbations can generate spurious or “false” eigenvalues. Thus, the study not only gives a sharp theoretical criterion for spectral stability but also clarifies the mechanism behind numerical spectral instability in non-selfadjoint quadratic models.

**Our Understanding of the Weyl Legacy**

Our world of mathematics and physics has been deeply shaped by the ideas of Hermann Weyl, one of the great thinkers of the twentieth century. The Weyl name appears in many important areas, from geometry and number theory to quantum mechanics and theoretical physics.

The work of Weyl helped connect abstract mathematics with the structure of the physical universe. His ideas about symmetry, space, and fields influenced later developments in modern physics, including gauge theory and the study of fundamental particles. In mathematics, Weyl’s contributions to group theory, representation theory, and differential geometry remain essential.

Our appreciation of Weyl’s legacy continues to grow because his ideas were not limited to one subject. The Weyl perspective shows how beauty, logic, and structure can come together to explain both mathematical truth and physical reality.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a mathematics research paper on pseudospectra and spectral stability of non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators defined by Weyl quantization.
counterfactuals.output:
We study pseudospectra and spectral stability for non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators on \(L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\) arising as Weyl quantizations \(q^{w}(x,D_x)\) of complex-valued elliptic quadratic forms \(q\) with \(\operatorname{Re} q\geq 0\). Although such operators have purely discrete spectrum determined by the Hamilton map associated with \(q\), their non-normality may produce large resolvent growth and severe spectral instability. We characterize regions of semiclassical pseudospectral instability in terms of the geometry of the numerical range of \(q\), the structure of the associated complex Hamilton flow, and the failure of normality of the quadratic symbol. In particular, we obtain sharp resolvent estimates in stable sectors and complementary lower bounds exhibiting rapid pseudospectral growth near critical boundary directions.

As an application, we prove quantitative spectral stability results for small lower-order and relatively bounded perturbations, identifying classes of perturbations for which eigenvalues remain stable and describing regimes where arbitrarily small perturbations may generate significant spectral displacement. The analysis combines exact quadratic operator calculus, FBI transform methods, and microlocal estimates adapted to complex phase space. These results give a precise description of the relationship between ellipticity, non-selfadjoint dynamics, and pseudospectral behavior for Weyl-quantized quadratic operators, extending the classical spectral theory of elliptic quadratic pencils to a robust stability framework.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a formal academic summary describing results on microlocal analysis, pseudospectrum, and spectral instability for elliptic quadratic operators with complex-valued quadratic Weyl symbols.
counterfactuals.output:
Elliptic quadratic differential operators with complex-valued Weyl symbols constitute a fundamental class of non-selfadjoint operators for which the interaction between microlocal geometry, pseudospectral behavior, and spectral instability can be described with considerable precision. Let  
\[
Q=q^w(x,D_x)
\]
denote the Weyl quantization of a complex-valued quadratic form \(q\) on phase space \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\), subject to an ellipticity condition such as
\[
q(X)=0,\ X\in \mathbb{R}^{2n}\quad \Longrightarrow \quad X=0.
\]
Although ellipticity implies that \(Q\) has discrete spectrum under suitable domain choices, the non-selfadjoint nature of the operator can produce highly unstable spectral behavior.

A central microlocal feature is that the symbol \(q\) is governed by its associated Hamilton map \(F\), defined through the polarization of \(q\) and the standard symplectic form \(\sigma\):
\[
q(X;Y)=\sigma(X,FY).
\]
The spectral structure of elliptic quadratic operators can often be expressed explicitly in terms of the eigenvalues of \(F\). In favorable cases, the spectrum consists of a lattice of eigenvalues determined by the eigenvalues of \(F\) with positive imaginary part, reflecting the exact solvability of quadratic models. Thus, unlike general non-selfadjoint elliptic operators, the point spectrum is algebraically tractable.

However, explicit spectral information does not imply spectral stability. A major conclusion of microlocal analysis in this setting is that non-normal elliptic quadratic operators may possess large pseudospectra. For a closed operator \(Q\), the \(\varepsilon\)-pseudospectrum is
\[
\operatorname{Spec}_{\varepsilon}(Q)
=
\left\{z\in \mathbb{C}:\|(Q-z)^{-1}\|>\varepsilon^{-1}\right\}
\cup \operatorname{Spec}(Q).
\]
Large pseudospectral regions indicate that the resolvent norm can grow rapidly far away from the actual spectrum. For complex elliptic quadratic operators, this growth is typically explained by the existence of semiclassical quasimodes localized near phase-space points where the symbol takes the value \(z\) and where the Hamiltonian geometry satisfies a non-degeneracy condition.

In semiclassical form, one studies
\[
Q_h=q^w(x,hD_x),
\qquad h\to 0^+.
\]
Microlocal constructions show that if \(z\) lies in the interior of the range of \(q\) and if the real and imaginary parts of \(q\) fail to commute in the sense that
\[
\{\operatorname{Re} q,\operatorname{Im} q\}(X)\neq 0
\]
at some point \(X\) with \(q(X)=z\), then there exist families \(u_h\) with \(\|u_h\|=1\) such that
\[
\|(Q_h-z)u_h\|=\mathcal{O}(h^N)
\]
for every \(N\), or even exponentially small in \(h\) in analytic settings. These quasimodes imply super-polynomial or exponential lower bounds on the resolvent norm:
\[
\|(Q_h-z)^{-1}\|\geq C_N h^{-N}
\]
for all \(N\), whenever the resolvent exists. Consequently, the pseudospectrum fills substantial regions of the symbol range, independently of the exact location of eigenvalues.

This phenomenon is a hallmark of spectral instability. Small perturbations of the operator, even of very small norm, can shift eigenvalues dramatically into regions where the unperturbed operator has no spectrum but large resolvent norm. Thus, the spectrum of a non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic operator is often a poor predictor of its behavior under perturbation, while the pseudospectrum provides a more accurate description of observable spectral properties.

The normal and nearly normal cases form an important contrast. If the real and imaginary parts of the quadratic symbol Poisson commute,
\[
\{\operatorname{Re} q,\operatorname{Im} q\}=0,
\]
then the operator exhibits more stable behavior, and the resolvent growth is more closely tied to the distance from the spectrum. In such cases, pseudospectral effects are weaker, reflecting the compatibility of the Hamiltonian flows generated by \(\operatorname{Re} q\) and \(\operatorname{Im} q\). The failure of this Poisson-commutation condition is therefore a microlocal mechanism for non-normality and pseudospectral instability.

Another important aspect concerns the geometry of the numerical range
\[
\Sigma(q)=\overline{q(\mathbb{R}^{2n})}.
\]
For elliptic quadratic forms, \(\Sigma(q)\) is typically a closed angular sector or a proper cone in the complex plane. The pseudospectral behavior is strongly influenced by the interior of \(\Sigma(q)\). Points lying inside the numerical range but away from the spectrum may nevertheless correspond to very large resolvent norms. Near the boundary of \(\Sigma(q)\), the behavior can be more delicate and depends on the degeneracy of the Hamiltonian flow and the order of contact of the real and imaginary parts of the symbol.

These results demonstrate that elliptic quadratic operators provide an exact yet nontrivial testing ground for the general theory of non-selfadjoint microlocal analysis. They combine explicit spectral formulas with highly nontrivial pseudospectral phenomena. The main conclusions may be summarized as follows:

1. **Discrete spectrum:** Ellipticity of the complex quadratic symbol implies discreteness of the spectrum under natural realizations of the Weyl quantized operator.

2. **Hamilton map spectral formula:** The eigenvalues of the operator can be described explicitly through the eigenvalues of the Hamilton map associated with the quadratic form.

3. **Microlocal quasimodes:** In regions of the symbol range where the Poisson bracket condition
   \[
   \{\operatorname{Re} q,\operatorname{Im} q\}\neq 0
   \]
   holds, one can construct highly accurate quasimodes.

4. **Large pseudospectra:** These quasimodes yield rapid resolvent growth, often super-polynomial or exponential in the semiclassical parameter.

5. **Spectral instability:** The spectrum is unstable under small perturbations, and the pseudospectrum gives a more reliable picture of the operator’s effective spectral behavior.

6. **Role of normality:** When the real and imaginary parts of the symbol commute microlocally, pseudospectral instability is reduced; when they do not, strong non-selfadjoint effects dominate.

Overall, the microlocal analysis of elliptic quadratic Weyl operators reveals a sharp distinction between spectral exactness and spectral stability. Even when the spectrum can be computed explicitly, the operator may display extreme sensitivity to perturbations due to large pseudospectra generated by nontrivial Hamiltonian geometry.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a journal-style abstract explaining a necessary and sufficient condition for spectral stability of non-selfadjoint quadratic differential operators, and what happens when the condition fails.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**  
We describe a necessary and sufficient condition for spectral stability of non-selfadjoint quadratic differential operators. Let  
\[
Q=q^w(x,D_x)
\]
be the Weyl quantization of a complex-valued quadratic form \(q\) on phase space, with ellipticity or partial ellipticity assumptions ensuring discrete spectrum. Spectral stability is governed by the geometry of the Hamilton dynamics of \(q\), or equivalently by the interaction between its real and imaginary parts. In the quadratic setting, stability holds precisely when the operator has no genuinely non-normal component: equivalently, after a complex linear symplectic change of variables, the quadratic form is reducible to a normal form for which the real and imaginary parts commute, or, in Hamiltonian terms, the relevant Poisson brackets vanish in the sense that the real and imaginary flows are compatible. In operator language, this amounts to the condition that \(Q\) be similar to a normal, in particular selfadjoint up to multiplication by a complex phase, quadratic oscillator.

When this condition is satisfied, the spectrum is robust: eigenvalues vary continuously under small perturbations, spectral projections remain uniformly controlled, and the resolvent does not exhibit large growth away from the spectrum. Thus the spectrum accurately reflects the behavior of the operator.

When the condition fails, the operator is spectrally unstable. Although the spectrum may remain discrete, the resolvent becomes very large far from the eigenvalues, producing large pseudospectra. As a consequence, arbitrarily small perturbations can create large movements of eigenvalues, and spectral projections typically grow rapidly, often exponentially along the spectrum. In this regime the spectrum alone is a poor descriptor of the dynamics; the pseudospectrum gives the correct picture of the operator’s instability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research paper abstract about false eigenvalues in numerical computations for non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic operators, connecting them to pseudospectral instability at high energies.
counterfactuals.output:
We study the occurrence of false eigenvalues in numerical approximations of non-selfadjoint elliptic quadratic differential operators. Although such operators have purely discrete spectra, their non-normality can produce severe spectral instability, causing standard discretization schemes to return spurious eigenvalues that do not converge to the true spectrum. We relate this phenomenon to the high-energy structure of the pseudospectrum. In particular, we show that, for elliptic quadratic operators whose numerical range has nontrivial interior, the resolvent may grow rapidly along large regions away from the spectrum, making computed spectra highly sensitive to discretization, roundoff error, and finite-dimensional truncation. These pseudospectral effects become increasingly pronounced at high energies, where numerical eigenvalues may accumulate along pseudospectral level sets rather than near genuine eigenvalues.

The analysis combines semiclassical rescaling, resolvent estimates, and finite-dimensional approximation arguments to characterize regimes in which spectral pollution is expected. We demonstrate that false eigenvalues are not merely artifacts of poorly conditioned algorithms but reflect intrinsic instability of the underlying non-selfadjoint problem. Model examples, including quadratic differential operators of rotated harmonic oscillator type, illustrate how high-energy pseudospectral regions govern the distribution of computed eigenvalues. The results emphasize the need for caution when interpreting numerical spectra of non-selfadjoint elliptic operators and suggest that pseudospectral diagnostics provide a more reliable framework for distinguishing true spectral features from computational artifacts.

counterfactuals.output:
We study the semiclassical pseudospectrum of non-selfadjoint differential operators whose principal symbols are complex-valued elliptic quadratic forms. For a quadratic operator
\[
P_h = q^w(x,hD_x), \qquad (x,\xi)\in \mathbb R^{2n},
\]
with \(\operatorname{Re} q\) elliptic and \(\operatorname{Im} q\) not assumed to satisfy any global sign condition, we give microlocal criteria for the existence of exponentially accurate quasimodes and derive corresponding lower bounds for the resolvent norm. The analysis is formulated in terms of the complex Hamilton map of \(q\) and the associated stratification of the range of the symbol by its symplectic geometry.

Our main result shows that, away from the boundary of the numerical range and outside a finite set of exceptional spectral points determined by the singular space, the semiclassical resolvent exhibits rapid pseudospectral growth:
\[
\|(P_h-z)^{-1}\| \geq C_N h^{-N}
\]
for every \(N\geq 1\), and in elliptic regions with nontrivial complex Hamilton flow this growth is in fact exponential in \(h^{-1}\). The construction relies on complex WKB solutions localized near doubly characteristic phase-space points and on a FBI transform reduction to weighted holomorphic spaces, where the quadratic structure permits an explicit normal form for the conjugated operator.

We further describe the transition between elliptic spectral stability and pseudospectral instability in terms of the Poisson geometry of \(\operatorname{Re}q\) and \(\operatorname{Im}q\). In particular, we identify the role of points satisfying
\[
\{\operatorname{Re}q,\operatorname{Im}q\}\neq 0
\]
as sources of microlocal instability and relate the failure of semiclassical subelliptic estimates to the appearance of large resolvent norms. As a consequence, we obtain sharp resolvent lower bounds in compact subsets of the interior of the semiclassical pseudospectrum and characterize the exceptional stable directions where the quadratic operator retains discrete spectral behavior.

These results provide a precise microlocal description of the pseudospectrum for complex elliptic quadratic differential operators and illustrate the extent to which non-normality, encoded by the Hamilton dynamics of the complex symbol, governs semiclassical spectral instability.
